title: Discovery of a new class of cell-penetrating peptides by novel phage display platform
one_line: Authors built a phage display selection (NNJA) that engineers a lysosomal cathepsin substrate into phage protein PIII so only phage escaping to the cytoplasm survive, yielding a new class of non-cationic cell-penetrating peptides.
key_claims: The cathepsin-cleavable PIII counter-selection eliminates lysosome-trapped phage, so selection outputs peptides optimised for cytoplasmic rather than endo-lysosomal delivery.
The discovered CPPs are nine amino acids long and lack the positive-charge clusters typical of classical CPPs.
Sequence enrichment showed methionine/leucine at position 1, serine/threonine at position 2, and proline in the middle and at the C-terminus.
The peptides delivered siRNA (with significant gene knockdown), antibodies, proteins and reporter molecules, with cytoplasmic localisation confirmed by confocal microscopy across multiple cell types.
Uptake was efficient without significant toxicity and comparable or superior to traditional CPPs such as TAT.
limitations: Work is cell-culture based; no in vivo validation, stability or pharmacokinetic data reported.
Mechanism of cell entry and endosomal escape is not resolved.
Tissue selectivity is only proposed as an adaptation of the platform, not demonstrated.
Cargo size limits were not defined.
Scale-up of peptide synthesis and cargo conjugation remains untested.
open_questions: Does an NNJA-derived peptide achieve cytoplasmic cargo delivery and target knockdown in vivo with acceptable pharmacokinetics?
What mechanism (receptor, endosomal escape route) distinguishes these non-cationic 9-mers from cationic CPPs?
Can the selection be re-run in different cell types to yield genuinely tissue-selective CPPs?
What is the maximum cargo size and conjugation chemistry compatible with cytoplasmic delivery?
